message:
feat(deploy): the publish procedure, as a script that refuses rather than hopes

There was no deployment script in the repository. The NAS has
.remote60-deploy-step.sh, but that builds the service the first time -- it creates
systemd units -- so it is not this. The original is the procedure that had only
ever been carried out by hand, and this encodes it.

The order is the whole point:

  preflight -> upload artifacts -> verify them ON THE SERVER -> back up the old
            -> swap manifest+sig atomically, LAST -> verify from outside

The manifest is what makes a release public. Publishing it first opens a window
in which the endpoint hands out a document naming files that 404, and a host that
reads it during that window reports a failed download rather than "not yet".

It refuses: an unverified signature; a manifest that does not describe the files
on disk; the same version with different bytes (a published URL is signed, so
changing the bytes behind it makes every signature for it a lie); a URL outside
the public base; a path outside the root; a second deploy while one holds the
lock.

Modes are set explicitly rather than inherited. gnlink's umask happens to be 0002
today, which gives o+rX -- but 0.2.108 spent an afternoon returning 403 for
exactly this, and "it works because of the umask we happen to have" is not a
property anyone verified. Backups go to a gnlink-owned path, because
/opt/gnlink/backups is root-owned and a backup that fails silently leaves
rollback with nothing; manifest and signature are kept as a pair, since a
manifest restored without its signature verifies as nothing.

The test suite runs the real script against an isolated root, 40 checks. It found
two defects while being written:

  - A SUCCESSFUL deploy left its lock behind: rmdir fails on a non-empty
    directory and the owner file was still there. A lock that survives success is
    worse than one that survives failure -- nothing looks wrong until the next
    release refuses to start for an unrelated-looking reason.
  - The hash-mismatch case tampered by appending, so the size check fired first.
    The assertion named the hash while the hash comparison never ran. It now
    flips one byte in place.

ssh and curl are not covered and are not pretended to be. So the real server was
exercised separately with --verify-only: 0.2.109's manifest is IDENTICAL, all
nine artifacts on the server match and are readable, and all nine fetch
anonymously over https and hash as signed. Nothing was re-published.
